title: Adapting Communication Without Losing the Meaning
audience: All staff; useful for supervisors giving instructions and feedback.

Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Adapting Communication Without Losing the Meaning
Making service information and workplace expectations clear while respecting different ways of communicating.
Intermediate self-directed learning
slides.narration: A message may seem clear to the person giving it while leaving someone else unsure about what matters. This course examines how shared context, directness, pauses, and opportunities to speak affect understanding in DSD work. You will consider a service conversation, an onboarding experience, and community feedback. The aim is to preserve the meaning of a message while making it easier to understand, question, and use. A different communication preference does not establish anyone’s ability or cultural identity.

slides.text:
The meaning you want to preserve
A service explanation carries facts, choices, and a relationship. A work instruction carries responsibilities and expectations.

Think of a message that assumes people already know the background. What would a newcomer need to understand it?
slides.narration: Consider the phrase, “Use the usual route.” A colleague with years of experience may hear a complete instruction. A new employee may not know which route, who receives the request, or what happens afterward. The issue is the information available to the listener. Privately, try replacing that phrase with the essential steps and a reason for using them. Keep the task’s actual meaning. Clearer wording should make the same responsibility understandable rather than introduce a different requirement.

slides.text:
Shared context and explicit information
Some meaning comes from words. Other meaning comes from shared history, relationships, or familiar references.

Communication can rely more or less on either source. The same person may communicate differently across situations.
slides.narration: High context and low context describe different degrees of reliance on shared information and explicit wording. They are useful questions about an exchange, rather than categories for judging a person. A reference that works among close colleagues may be unclear in a first service conversation. Likewise, a person may first explain a relationship because it gives the request meaning. Look at what the message depends on and what the listener can actually know. Avoid assigning a style from someone’s community or nationality.

slides.text:
A service explanation with room to respond
A person describes family routines before asking about support. Staff acknowledge the concern and explain the available next step.

Asking what remains unclear gives the person room to connect that information to daily life.
slides.narration: Imagine a person explaining that several relatives share support across different days. A quick list of service terms could miss why they described that arrangement. Staff can acknowledge its importance, explain the relevant next step, and ask which part needs clarification. The explanation stays accurate while recognizing the person’s context. We still do not know every service requirement or what support will be appropriate. The immediate task is understanding the request well enough to respond responsibly, without deciding that a longer account is irrelevant.

slides.text:
Practice: a longer service account
A person describes family support routines before asking about a service. Staff are ready to interrupt because the explanation seems too long. Which response best preserves useful meaning?
A. Acknowledge the concern, explain the relevant next step, and ask what needs clarification.
B. Skip the account and repeat the service terms more firmly.
C. Use a culture brief to decide why the person gives so much background.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: This fictional conversation asks you to distinguish an unfamiliar way of explaining a concern from an irrelevant concern. The family account may help staff understand how support works, but it may also include information beyond the immediate question. We cannot decide which without listening and clarifying. Consider what each response would make possible. Would it preserve an accurate explanation and a chance to respond, or move ahead on an assumption? You are choosing the next communication response, rather than determining eligibility or promising a particular service.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Acknowledge the concern, explain the relevant next step, and ask what needs clarification.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Skip the account and repeat the service terms more firmly.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Use a culture brief to decide why the person gives so much background.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
The account may contain information about how support works in daily life. Acknowledgment and clarification can connect the service explanation to that situation. The need and appropriate response still require evidence; the length of the account does not settle them.

What information could be lost if longer accounts are routinely cut short?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The first response preserves room to understand the request. Recognizing the concern does not require accepting every detail as necessary or promising a service outcome. Staff can explain the relevant step and ask what remains unclear. The person’s response may identify useful context or another question. That is stronger evidence than assuming that a long account means poor understanding.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Repeating terms without hearing their relevance could leave the person unsure how to proceed. If repeated, this routine may keep important circumstances out of service discussions. Clarify the request and essential information before deciding that background has no value.

What information could be lost if longer accounts are routinely cut short?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A firm repetition may sound clear while failing to explain what the terms mean for this situation. If people who give more context are repeatedly cut short, their circumstances may enter the record less fully than those of people using familiar terms. That possible barrier deserves examination. One conversation cannot establish its prevalence or explain every service difficulty.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A brief may prepare questions, but it cannot explain this individual. Using it as proof could replace the actual concern with a group assumption. Hear the person’s meaning and examine the relevant service information before choosing a response.

What information could be lost if longer accounts are routinely cut short?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A culture brief can suggest that relationships and shared responsibilities may matter, but it does not tell us what this person intends. Treating it as an explanation can make a stereotype seem like understanding. A more useful response asks about the service concern directly and allows the person to correct staff’s interpretation without supplying a personal cultural history.

slides.text:
Information that insiders take for granted
References such as “the usual process” can hide a contact, decision, or next step.

Explain the background needed for the task. A newcomer should not have to reveal personal history to receive a usable explanation.
slides.narration: In onboarding, experienced colleagues may share shortcuts that feel efficient. The new employee sees the same message but lacks its history. If asking for clarification is treated as poor preparation, the employee may stop asking and miss useful opportunities. That consequence is possible, not established by one unclear instruction. Making the relevant background available can help people contribute sooner. The question is what the task requires them to know, not whether they already speak as comfortably as people who helped create the process.

slides.text:
Directness and intended meaning
A sentence may state a request directly or suggest it through a concern, question, or observation.

“The next step is unclear” may be feedback, a request for explanation, or both. Ask before deciding.
slides.narration: Direct and indirect communication concern how the words relate to the intended message. An indirect phrase is not necessarily evasive, and direct wording is not necessarily unfriendly. A staff member who hears a concern can ask, “Would it help if I explained what happens next?” That question checks a possible meaning without demanding a different speaking style. The answer may identify another issue entirely. Keep the person’s response open enough to correct your interpretation rather than simply confirm it.

slides.text:
Clear requests and honest choices
Explain what is required, what is optional, and what you can offer.

A warm invitation should not disguise a requirement. A clear requirement should still explain its purpose and allow relevant questions.
slides.narration: Suppose a meeting invitation asks people to offer comments, but the decision has already been made. Friendly wording alone cannot create a meaningful choice. Explain whether comments can change the proposal or help clarify implementation. In services, similarly distinguish a required step from a suggestion that the person may decline. Being explicit can support understanding without becoming harsh. You preserve the relationship by being honest about the choice available, and by listening to questions about how someone can use it.

slides.text:
Pauses and opportunities to speak
Silence may reflect thought, uncertainty, interpretation, preference, or something else. Its meaning remains unknown until clarified.

Leave room for a response. Ask whether the person wants more time, an explanation, or another way to contribute.
slides.narration: A pause tells us that speech has stopped; it does not tell us why. Quickly answering for someone may save seconds while losing their perspective. In a development conversation, an employee might be considering how to disagree with a supervisor. In a service conversation, a person might be connecting information to a daily routine. Offer a manageable opportunity to respond without demanding an explanation for the pause. Speaking speed alone does not establish understanding, commitment, or the quality of an idea.

slides.text:
Onboarding without hidden expectations
A new colleague is told to “bring it through the usual channel.” Nobody explains that channel or how questions are welcomed.

Naming the contact and next step makes the instruction usable. It also keeps uncertainty from being mistaken for poor performance.
slides.narration: During onboarding, people are learning both their responsibilities and the workplace’s unstated habits. A new colleague may hesitate to interrupt because they are unsure how questions will be received. A supervisor can explain the instruction and invite clarification without diagnosing that hesitation. If unexplained expectations recur, employees with familiar networks may gain an advantage in assignments and recognition. To understand the pattern, examine which information was shared, how questions were answered, and what opportunities followed. One delayed task alone cannot establish the cause.

slides.text:
Practice: the usual channel
A new employee misses a step after being told to use “the usual channel.” A supervisor interprets the delay as poor initiative. What would give the fairest basis for the next conversation?
A. Ask why the employee did not copy the experienced staff’s approach.
B. Explain the channel, check what information was available, and hear the employee’s question.
C. Treat hesitation as a cultural preference and avoid discussing the task.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The employee’s missed step is known, but the reason needs examination. A supervisor may be accustomed to a process that was never explained to the newcomer. The employee may also have misunderstood an explicit part of the instruction. Both possibilities can be considered without deciding character or culture in advance. Think about which response makes the relevant information available while retaining the employee’s responsibility for the task. Then consider what could happen if the same unexplained expectations influence assignments and recognition throughout onboarding and development.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Ask why the employee did not copy the experienced staff’s approach.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Explain the channel, check what information was available, and hear the employee’s question.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Treat hesitation as a cultural preference and avoid discussing the task.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Copying experienced colleagues may depend on access to informal knowledge. Treating that access as initiative can leave an unclear instruction unexamined. Ask what the colleague knew and clarify the actual step before drawing a performance conclusion.

How could unequal access to informal knowledge affect later development opportunities?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The first answer keeps familiar behavior as the standard without examining whether the newcomer could know what to copy. Informal knowledge may be useful, but unequal access to it can affect who completes tasks confidently and gains further opportunities. The next conversation should examine what the instruction actually communicated, rather than assume that a missed step reflects poor initiative.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This response examines both the instruction and the employee’s understanding. It makes the task usable without changing the responsibility. If unclear onboarding recurs, compare access to information and later opportunities; this delay alone does not establish a broader pattern.

How could unequal access to informal knowledge affect later development opportunities?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The second answer provides a clearer basis for judgment because it examines the actual instruction and the employee’s account. Clarifying a step does not remove responsibility for completing it. It helps distinguish an information gap from another issue. If similar gaps recur, the relevant question is whose access to guidance and opportunities differs, and what evidence explains that difference.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A cultural explanation is unsupported and may prevent useful guidance. The task still needs discussion. Clarify the expectation and invite relevant questions, without assigning a communication style or requiring a personal explanation.

How could unequal access to informal knowledge affect later development opportunities?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The third answer replaces one assumption with another. We do not know that cultural preference explains hesitation, and avoiding the task would withhold useful guidance. A respectful discussion can clarify both the responsibility and the opportunity to ask questions. Cultural learning should improve understanding, rather than make ordinary work expectations unavailable to someone presumed to communicate differently.

slides.text:
Checking understanding respectfully
Invite the person to discuss how the explanation fits the task or what still needs clarification.

A respectful check examines the explanation as well as the listener. Agreement, silence, and a polite thank-you do not settle comprehension.
slides.narration: One useful question is, “How does that next step fit what you are trying to do?” It invites the person to connect the information with their purpose. Another is, “Which part should I explain differently?” Neither assumes the person failed to understand. In services, avoid making a demonstration of knowledge an extra condition for assistance. In the workplace, keep actual assessment responsibilities clear. A conversation about understanding should help locate the missing information, rather than become a test of whether someone communicates in the expected way.

slides.text:
Communication and access needs
Communication preferences and access needs may overlap, but neither should be guessed from a group label.

Ask what helps the person receive and respond to the information. Follow the appropriate language and accessibility arrangements.
slides.narration: Someone may need an accessible format, language assistance, a different communication method, or simply a clearer explanation. These possibilities are not interchangeable, and appearance or accent cannot establish the answer. Ask a relevant question about receiving and responding to the information, then follow the appropriate arrangements for the actual need. Adjusting directness alone will not fix an inaccessible document. Conversely, an accessible document may still assume insider knowledge. Examine both what information is available and whether the person can use it.

slides.text:
Community knowledge before assumptions
Culture briefs can prepare thoughtful questions about relationships and communication. They do not explain an individual’s preference.

Hear different community perspectives, including people less often reached by familiar partners.
slides.narration: A brief may remind staff to consider how relationships affect a service conversation. It cannot establish that every person from a community prefers the same explanation. Community engagement offers an opportunity to learn about actual experiences with the message and the process it describes. People may disagree, and that disagreement can be useful. Notice whose perspectives are missing because of the meeting format, language, location, or invitation. A familiar partner’s approval does not stand for everyone who may need the information.

slides.text:
Feedback that changes an explanation
Participants say a service letter names an action but leaves the response unclear. Staff examine what follows that action.

A revision can explain the next step and who responds, while keeping the actual process accurate.
slides.narration: Imagine community participants reviewing a letter that asks people to send information. The letter lists an address but does not explain what happens after the information arrives. Staff initially see a complete instruction; participants see an unanswered question about accountability. The appropriate response is to examine the actual process and explain it accurately. A revised letter is a change in communication, but its usefulness remains open to review. We would still need to know whether different intended readers can find and use that explanation.

slides.text:
Comparing ways to say the same thing
Try rewriting an unclear message in two ways: one with helpful background and one with concise explicit steps.

Keep the facts, choices, and responsibilities the same. Consider what each version makes easier to understand.
slides.narration: Use a fictional instruction such as, “Send it back and we will follow up.” One revision might explain why the information is needed and what the response will involve. Another might state the contact, sequence, and next step more concisely. Both should preserve the same actual meaning. Examine whether either version accidentally promises a decision, removes a choice, or hides uncertainty. This private exercise lets you compare communication choices without asking a colleague or service user to disclose personal experiences for the sake of learning.

slides.text:
Practice: a letter’s missing next step
Community participants say a service letter does not explain what follows after they send information. Staff say the address is correct. Which response would best address the concern?
A. Keep the letter because a correct address makes the instruction complete.
B. Ask one familiar partner whether most people in the community would understand it.
C. Check the actual response process, explain it accurately, and invite feedback on the revision.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The disagreement concerns what counts as a usable explanation. Staff have checked the address; participants are asking what happens afterward and who will respond. Neither question has to cancel the other. Consider whether the proposed response addresses the specific information gap and preserves accuracy. Then think about the pattern if letters repeatedly assume that readers know the organization’s internal process. People with familiar contacts may obtain an explanation that others cannot. That is a possible mechanism to examine, rather than a conclusion established by this single review.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Keep the letter because a correct address makes the instruction complete.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Ask one familiar partner whether most people in the community would understand it.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Check the actual response process, explain it accurately, and invite feedback on the revision.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The address may be correct while the next step remains unclear. Repeatedly treating accuracy as sufficient can leave people dependent on insider explanations. Examine the specific missing information and whether intended readers can use the instruction.

How could a clear letter still leave the service process difficult to use?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A correct address is important, but it does not answer the concern about what follows. Leaving that question unexplained may make the process harder to use and increase dependence on informal contacts. If the pattern recurs, examine which readers obtain the missing information and what consequences follow. The present feedback identifies a gap; it does not establish everyone’s experience.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
One partner’s view can be useful, but it cannot establish every reader’s experience. Different participants may identify different gaps. Hear the specific concern, examine the process, and seek appropriate perspectives beyond the most familiar voice.

How could a clear letter still leave the service process difficult to use?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A familiar partner may contribute relevant knowledge, but no one person can validate the experience of an entire community. Depending only on the easiest contact can preserve the same gaps in whose perspectives are heard. The more useful approach examines the specific concern and considers different experiences with the letter, without asking anyone to represent all people who might receive it.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This response links community feedback to a concrete revision. It preserves the process’s actual meaning and allows further correction. The revised letter’s usefulness remains unknown until there is evidence from people trying to understand and use it.

How could a clear letter still leave the service process difficult to use?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Checking the actual process and explaining it accurately connects the feedback to a meaningful change. Inviting review keeps the explanation open to correction. It still does not prove that every barrier is resolved: people may understand the step but face difficulty completing it. Keep communication evidence distinct from evidence about the service process, and consider both when deciding what remains to address.

slides.text:
When a familiar style becomes a rule
If quick, confident speech repeatedly determines whose ideas are heard, relevant knowledge may be overlooked.

Examine who receives time, clarification, and credit before deciding what explains a pattern.
slides.narration: A team may sincerely welcome ideas while repeatedly moving ahead when the fastest speaker finishes. The routine can give confident, familiar speakers more influence even when quieter colleagues have relevant information. Over time, that difference may affect assignments, development, and recognition. The possible mechanism is visible: the way turns are allocated changes whose knowledge enters decisions. To examine it, look at actual opportunities to contribute and what happened to those contributions. A difference in speaking style does not itself prove a systemic inequity.

slides.text:
A fairer way to hear relevant knowledge
Offer clear questions, usable information, and more than one appropriate way to contribute.

Maintain the task’s purpose. Review whether contributions are understood and considered rather than counting invitations alone.
slides.narration: An alternative might be to explain the decision question before a meeting, allow a considered response during the discussion, and provide another appropriate route for comments. These choices should fit the work rather than become a universal procedure. The important question is whether relevant knowledge can enter the decision. Sending more invitations alone will not show that. Examine whether people could use the information, whether their contributions were understood, and whether the eventual choice addresses the concerns that were raised.

slides.text:
Communication across the employee life cycle
Recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention all involve explaining expectations and hearing different perspectives.

Review whether familiar wording or speaking habits become an unstated condition for opportunity.
slides.narration: Communication matters before an employee joins and throughout their time in DSD. A recruitment notice may assume knowledge of government terms. Onboarding may rely on personal networks. Supervision may mistake a restrained response for agreement. Development decisions may reward the most familiar presentation style. These are different situations, not proof of a single cause. Their shared question is whether the essential information and opportunity to respond are available. Examine each routine in relation to its purpose, the relevant evidence, and the opportunities that followed.

slides.text:
What remains uncertain
A clearer explanation may improve understanding, but the effect needs evidence from the people using it.

Different accounts can reveal a remaining gap. Stay open to revising the message and your interpretation.
slides.narration: After changing an explanation, you may learn that one concern was resolved while another remains. Someone may understand the next step but still be unable to use it because of a service or workplace barrier. That information matters. It keeps a communication improvement from being mistaken for a complete solution. Consider what the response establishes and what remains unknown. Useful evidence might include the specific questions people still ask and their ability to act on the explanation, handled through the appropriate work responsibilities.

slides.text:
Communication that preserves understanding
Make essential meaning available. Ask before interpreting a communication difference.

Keep choices honest and access needs in view.

Notice whether repeated speaking habits influence whose information and ideas shape decisions.
slides.narration: Clear communication involves judgment rather than a single approved style. You can explain essential information directly, recognize relevant context, and make room for a response. You can also revise an interpretation when someone tells you it missed their meaning. Across service delivery and workplace culture, these choices help people use information and contribute what they know. As you leave this course, consider one fictional message you would now explain differently, why that change may help, and what you would still need to learn about its effect.

outcomes: Explain how shared context, directness, pauses, and turn-taking can affect understanding.
Ask a clarifying question without assigning a communication style to a community.
Compare two ways to explain the same service or work expectation while preserving its meaning.
Identify a participation rule that rewards familiar speech rather than relevant knowledge.
